newsitem.title: UK: Stg recovers its footing amid trade, CBI data.
newsitem.headline: Stg recovers its footing amid trade, CBI data.

text.p: Sterling recovered its footing after comments made by Bank of England governor Eddie George on Wednesday triggered profit taking and undermined the pound from seven-and-a-half-year peaks against the mark.

The pound ceded almost four of the eight pfennigs it had racked up against the mark in the past two trading days after George told a parliamentary committee that part of its rise against other major currencies was irrational.
Its slide was stemmed after a trade report on Thursday contained little evidence that the strength of the pound is feeding through into a widening in Britain's trade deficit.
A survey published later by the Confederation of British Industry backed up the recent chorus of complaints by exporters.
Sterling proved resilient, though, as the dollar bobbed back up towards the 71-month high it set against the mark yesterday.

"Profit taking and the fall out from Eddie George's comments has seen sterling come off a bit but it is still pretty expensive and wanting to get even more expensive," said Peter von Maydell, currency strategist at UBS.
Sterling was at 3.0626/36 marks at 1050 GMT from 3.0610/20 late Wednesday in Europe and the 3.0878 high it set yesterday. Cable was at $1.6740/45 from $1.6790/00 on Wednesday.
Sterling has surged 26 percent in trade-weighted terms in less than a year, eroding UK exporters' competitiveness and the value of their foreign-currency earnings.
Imperial Chemical Industries Plc was the latest in a series of companies to protest against its strength.

Its chief financial officer Alan Spall said in an interview with Reuters that sterling "was well overvalued above three marks" and that the company would be much more comfortable with it trading in the region of 2.50 to 2.60 marks.
A quarterly survey by the CBI highlighted British exporters woes.

It showed UK manufacturing orders in the four months to July fell at their fastest rate since October 1991, while optimism about exports for the year ahead fell at its fastest rate since October 1980, the CBI said. Meantime, its index of business confidence entered negative territory for first time since April 1996.
"Exporters have every right to complain and things will get a lot worse if sterling remains strong," said UBS's von Maydell.

This deterioration has yet to show up in UK trade data, though. Britain's global trade deficit fell to 508 million pounds in May from 989 million in April and the non-EU deficit rose to 713 million pounds in June from 563 million in May.
Both numbers were better than economists had expected and helped the pound claw back ground against the mark.

Sterling's recent gains against the mark have primarily been driven by dollar gains and mark weakness. While traders are looking for the pound to push higher, an element of wariness is creeping in about how much further it can gain on the dollar's coattails.

"Fundamentally sterling is well bid but I am beginning to get nervous about it given that dollar/mark is approaching key levels which might lead to G7 intervention," said Adam Cribben, assistant chief trader at Credit Lyonnais.
